prompt.context: A large fast food chain has hired Bain to improve the company's profitability. You're about to have an initial brainstorming session with your team around your client's options, and you want to collect your thoughts first.
prompt.question: What structure would you use to approach the profitability problem, and how would you begin identifying levers to improve profitability?

clarifying_info.q: Is the client able to raise prices?
clarifying_info.a: The customer is price sensitive, and the market is fairly saturated.

clarifying_info.q: Are fixed costs a significant lever?
clarifying_info.a: The fixed costs are pretty stable.

clarifying_info.q: How many restaurants does the client have?
clarifying_info.a: The client is similar to McDonald's in terms of the number of outlets.

clarifying_info.q: What does a case of napkins cost the client?
clarifying_info.a: A case of 6,000 napkins costs the client $28, so roughly $0.005 per napkin.

framework: State profit equation: Profit = Revenue - Costs
Revenue = Price x Quantity; Costs = Fixed Costs + Variable Costs
Revenue levers: price increases (limited by price-sensitive market), volume growth (new/existing branches), creative revenue streams (e.g., catering contracts)
Cost levers: fixed costs (sell branches/real estate — but stable), variable costs (raw materials and packaging) — focus here given stable fixed costs and saturated market
Narrow to variable costs: raw materials and packaging are the main buckets to investigate

questions.prompt: After ruling out price increases and fixed cost reductions, identify the major variable cost buckets the client should focus on.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify raw materials and packaging as the two primary variable cost buckets. Variable costs are a function of price and volume, so levers are: negotiate lower prices with suppliers (e.g., consolidate purchasing), find cheaper alternatives, or reduce volume used. For raw materials, reducing quantity risks changing recipes (competitive advantage). For packaging, creative options include changing container shape/size, reducing packaging weight, consolidating family packaging, reducing color/logo detail.

questions.prompt: Bain has identified a new napkin dispensing technology that could reduce the number of napkins each customer takes. How much money could the client save per year in the US by switching to the new napkin dispensers in all restaurants?
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify and estimate: number of restaurants, customer visits per store per year, napkins used per customer before and after switch, and price per napkin. Walk through each assumption explicitly and show the multiplication.

math.setup: Savings = (napkins saved per customer) x (price per napkin) x (customers per day) x (days per year) x (number of restaurants)
steps: Number of restaurants: assume 1 McDonald's per 20,000-25,000 Americans; US population ~275M → 11,000-13,750 restaurants; use ~12,000
Customers per day: 20,000 catchment visits twice a month = 40,000 visits/month / 30 days ≈ 1,333/day; actual benchmark ~1,500/day; use 1,500
Napkins per customer: old dispensers ~5 napkins; new prohibitive dispensers ~2 napkins; savings = 3 napkins per customer

questions.prompt: How would you pressure-check the $98.6M estimate and what factors should you flag for your manager?
questions.guidance: To pressure-check: compare napkin expense as a % of a comparable company's operating income; find out what the client currently spends per restaurant per year on napkins. Key flags: (1) large chain likely gets a volume discount — $0.005/napkin may overstate price; (2) up to 50% of customers are drive-through — their napkin behavior may not change, reducing savings by up to 50%; (3) the three-napkin reduction estimate is unvalidated — a pilot program is needed.

questions.prompt: Assume 10 dispensers are needed per store for 120,000 dispensers total. The new dispensers require proprietary napkins costing $0.01 each (vs. $0.005 currently). At what maximum price per dispenser would the investment still be worthwhile?
questions.guidance: Set total cost of new system equal to total cost of old system and solve for dispenser price. New system cost = dispenser investment + new napkin spend. Old napkin spend is the baseline. Solve: 120,000 x D + (new napkin cost) = (old napkin cost). The break-even dispenser price is the answer; any price above it makes the investment not worth doing.

steps: Old total napkin cost = 5 x $0.005 x 1,500 x 365 x 12,000 = $164.25M
New napkin cost (2 napkins at $0.01) = 2 x $0.01 x 1,500 x 365 x 12,000 = $131.4M
math.answer: Maximum price per dispenser is ~$273 (actual dispenser cost is ~$50, well below this threshold — investment is clearly worthwhile)

questions.prompt: Given that the dispensers cost ~$50, what other factors should the client consider before deciding to switch?
questions.guidance: Candidate should think through both qualitative advantages and disadvantages, then suggest how to evaluate them.

brainstorming.prompt: What creative ways could the client reduce packaging costs specifically?

categories.name: Container design
ideas: Change shape or size of food containers to use less material
Consolidate family packaging into fewer pieces
Reduce weight of packaging while maintaining food protection

categories.name: Branding/aesthetics
ideas: Reduce degree of color printing on packaging
Reduce logo prevalence without sacrificing brand recognition

categories.name: Consumables
ideas: Lock bathrooms so non-customers do not waste toilet paper and towels
Reduce size or number of napkins purchased

categories.name: Supplier negotiation
ideas: Negotiate lower prices with packaging suppliers

recommendation: Switch to new napkin dispensers at ~$50/unit — well below the $273 break-even price — generating up to ~$32.85M in net annual savings
Negotiate volume-based pricing with the new napkin/dispenser supplier and include contract caps on future price increases
Pursue supplier consolidation and renegotiation across all raw material and packaging categories as the broader variable cost reduction program
risks: Up to 50% drive-through customers may see no napkin reduction, cutting savings by up to 50%
Locking into a single paper manufacturer reduces buyer power and exposes client to future price hikes
Customers may perceive restrictive dispensers as poor service, especially after spills — brand/satisfaction risk
The 3-napkin-per-customer savings assumption is unvalidated and should be confirmed via pilot
next_steps: Run a pilot program in a sample of stores to validate napkin reduction (3 napkins/customer) and measure customer reaction
Negotiate a multi-year contract with the dispenser/paper supplier including price caps before full rollout
Conduct a broader variable cost audit across raw materials and packaging using Bain's value-focused approach
